item.title: Ledger Wallet Hidden Spy Chip
item.description:
Crypto worth more than 86 million dollars was drained from Ledger wallets. Each confirmed case was a wallet bought from a shop Ledger had authorized itself. Inside one of them sat a second circuit board.

On October 9, an on-chain investigator who goes by Specter posted a list of ten crypto addresses on X. Ledger users had been reporting empty wallets online, and he followed the stolen funds on Bitcoin, Ethereum and TRON back to where they came from. Money had flowed in from victim wallets, and his count came to more than 86 million dollars. How many wallets that was, he wrote later that day, he could not tell yet.

About an hour later, Ledger posted that it was looking into losses among users in Southeast Asia who had bought their Ledger from one reseller, CryptoBilis. It had asked CryptoBilis to stop selling and shipping Ledger devices. Buyers from the last 90 days were told not to set their device up, and buyers who already had were advised to move their crypto to a new Ledger with a new recovery phrase.

The next day, Ledger wrote: “Ledger can confirm that one of the impacted users’ devices contained an unauthorized hardware implant.” From then on, its advice covered buyers from CryptoBilis whenever they had bought: do not set the device up.

CryptoBilis, an authorized Ledger reseller in Malaysia, Indonesia and the Philippines, stopped selling hardware wallets. On October 11, Ledger said the number of affected devices is limited, and that each confirmed case so far is a device sold through CryptoBilis. How much was stolen, Ledger has not confirmed.

A hardware wallet stores the key to your crypto inside a special chip, the secure element, made to resist people who try to pull secrets out of it with lab equipment. When you set the wallet up, it shows you 24 recovery words one time, so you can write them down. With those words, the wallet and the crypto in it can be rebuilt on another device. To show them, the secure element sends them to the small screen. On a Nano X that goes over three thin wires, a connection called the SPI bus, as plain data without any encryption.

Researchers at Tibane Labs tapped those wires on a Nano X themselves while it started up. From the data they caught, they rebuilt the screen exactly as it was drawn, down to the Ledger logo 734.6 milliseconds in. The recovery words travel over the same wires.

The implant is connected to those three wires. It is a small extra board with its own processor, added to a wallet that came out of Ledger’s own factory. Its processor reads along with the screen, picks out the letters and keeps the words. A mobile modem on the same board, with its own SIM card and antenna, then sends them to the attacker. For the owner, nothing changes. The wallet works as it always did, and Ledger’s genuine check, the one that tells you the device is genuine, still passes, because the secure element did come from Ledger.

On October 13, Ledger’s own security lab, Ledger Donjon, described the implant in the CryptoBilis wallets the same way. It sits inside the case and reads what is shown on the screen. When the wallet displays the 24 recovery words during setup, its microcontroller, the small processor on the extra board, decodes them. It then sends them out over LTE, the 4G mobile network, through an eSIM, a SIM card built in as a chip. Ledger says it is a separate component that does not change the secure element, the operating system or the transactions.

The researchers who tapped the screen wires have followed this implant through three versions so far, and each one is harder to spot than the one before.

The first turned up in August 2025, in a Reddit thread warning about a “Nano X” sold to steal crypto. Joe Grand of Grand Idea Studio, a hardware hacker, got hold of that device, took it apart and showed what was inside at the hardwear.io USA 2026 conference. It was a prototype, with thin enamel-coated copper wires running from the screen lines to a small add-on board, glued in where part of the battery used to be. To make room, the battery had been shrunk to 70 mAh. A fixed 10 kΩ resistor replaced its temperature sensor, and the battery gauge was bypassed, so the wallet always showed a full battery. Its firmware held the shapes of the letters a to z, matched the screen data against them and stored the recovery words. The modem used an eSIM, and that eSIM carried a Vodafone NL “DATA ONLY” profile.

The first known implant that read the recovery words off a Ledger’s screen went out over a Dutch data SIM.

In September 2026 the researchers got hold of two newer ones. The first came from Yahoo! Auctions in Japan, and the loose wires were gone. In their place was a flat flex circuit, the kind you order from a board factory, laid across the back of the Ledger’s board. It was soldered onto the factory test pads, the small contact points a board gets tested on before it leaves the factory. Those pads gave the implant power from the wallet’s battery and a view of the data going to the screen, which means whoever made it had the test pad layout of the Nano X in hand. The battery was swapped for a smaller one again, this time with no markings and no protection circuit, so there was nothing to stop it from overcharging or shorting. The chip that runs this implant carries a date code that, in the chip maker’s usual format, reads as week 51 of 2025, months after that first warning.

The other one came from Amazon Japan, from a seller based in China, in a parcel shipped from Malaysia. Open the case with the screen still in place and it looks like an ordinary Nano X, with the original battery and the original board. The only thing out of place is a thin black antenna wire along the top edge. Under the screen sat the modem, a microcontroller and an eSIM. A foam pad normally cushions the back of the display, and the builders tore it out to make room, so the battery could stay as it was. They coated the implant board the same black as the Ledger’s own board, so it doesn’t stand out when the case is opened. They also scraped the tops of the microcontroller and the eSIM until the part numbers were gone.

The modem kept its markings. It is a Nordic nRF9151, an ordinary part sold for low power mobile networks. In its maker’s usual format, its date code reads as week 39 of 2025, so it is also newer than the first warning.

The antenna was made for the Nano X alone. It is a thin printed strip that follows the inside of the case, with its own part number printed on it: AC-A2016-NANO-V1.1. NANO is the target, and V1.1 means there was already a version before it. The implant board is cut around the Ledger’s own parts, so it drops straight into place without measuring and with hardly any skill, and the researchers describe it as built for mass installation.

Photos of an implant hidden under the screen were online before the drains. On September 16, three weeks before the first reports, Mark Karpelès, the former CEO of the Mt. Gox Bitcoin exchange, posted them. He had bought his Nano X outside Ledger’s recommended channels, on a well known platform, from a Chinese seller, at close to half the normal price, and it was shipped from Malaysia. “The new implant is hidden by the screen, so I would expect some people may miss it,” he wrote, and the easiest tell, according to him, is the antenna cable.

On October 13, he posted that a Ledger Flex, bought this summer at Singapore airport, also contained a spy implant. The buyer had seen scratches on the case, never plugged it in and sent it to him instead.

The reports now reach Europe too. On October 12, a user who goes by Johannes posted on X that he had bought a Ledger at two different MediaMarkt stores, and that both had extra cables and an LTE module inside. According to a store employee, he wrote, the second one was not a return. His post passed 1.5 million views. A day later, MediaMarktSaturn told Cointelegraph it has removed all of the manufacturer’s products from its stores and online platforms. On mediamarkt.nl, a search for Ledger no longer turns up a single Ledger wallet.

Ledger itself wrote on October 13 that MediaMarkt Saturn stopped selling Ledger devices with its agreement, after one customer in Germany reported an implant, and that no loss of funds was reported. It has not confirmed that implant or the one in the Flex. It says it has not verified a drain tied to a wallet bought outside CryptoBilis, and that it is reviewing reports of implants in other models and locations.

CryptoBilis changed hands this year. Its former co-founders told the researchers that new owners bought the company earlier in 2026, and that they have had no access to it since the handover. A post on X, citing screenshots from the company registry that the researchers have not verified, says it passed in August 2026 to a shareholder with an address in China. The second implant the researchers bought was shipped from Malaysia, where CryptoBilis is based. The researchers mention that, and in the same breath say they have no evidence linking the two. They have not tested a device sold by CryptoBilis, and a change of owners does not prove anything.

In cybersecurity, attribution is one of the hardest problems. Parts are sold openly, and a seller can sit in one country and ship from another. The researchers also point out that an implanted wallet doesn’t need the attacker to sell it, because ordinary resale moves it along. What we know for sure is how these implants work. Who put one in the wallet Ledger examined is still unknown, and Ledger says it is working with the authorities to find out.

Ledger also wrote that this threat reaches past Ledger to the rest of the industry. It asked others to work together on keeping track of devices from the factory to the buyer and on making tampering harder. Its own authorized resellers and distributors were told to buy stock only through authorized channels, and never to put returned products back on the shelf. A returned box has already been in someone else’s hands.

So the secure element did what Ledger built it for, and the key stayed inside the chip. The implant only needed the one moment the chip shows the 24 words to a person, and copied them on their way to the screen. The wires to the display and anything soldered next to them are outside the chip’s reach, and the genuine check only asks the chip whether the chip is genuine.

The implant gets its chance during setup, when the 24 words are on the screen. A wallet that has not been set up has not shown them yet. Once the words have been on the screen of a wallet like this, assume someone else has them too, even if the wallet never touched a computer. The only way out is a new recovery phrase, created on a device you trust, with your crypto moved over to it. Ledger now also says never to enter or restore a recovery phrase on a wallet bought from CryptoBilis.

What you can do:

  • → Bought from CryptoBilis and not set up yet: don’t set it up, and contact Ledger Support
  • → Already set up: move your crypto promptly to a new wallet with a new recovery phrase
  • → Never enter or restore a recovery phrase on a wallet bought from CryptoBilis
  • → Lost crypto or holding a tampered wallet: keep the device and its packaging, don’t reset it, file a police report, and talk to the police before you open it or send it off
  • → Buy a hardware wallet from the maker itself, and walk away from one sold far below the normal price
  • → Bought elsewhere and want to look inside: back up your 24 words first, because opening a wallet can damage it, and follow Ledger’s own inspection guide
  • → Changpeng Zhao, the founder of Binance, advises leaving a new hardware wallet for a couple of weeks before you move a meaningful amount to it, and following the news in that time
  • → Ledger will never call you, message you or ask for your 24 words, and scammers use incidents like this one to try
  • → Information about the people behind this goes to security@ledger.com

Your other devices use your own network instead of a hidden SIM, and you can learn to read exactly what each of them sends. item.title: Denmark CPR Breach Took 8.7 Million ID Numbers Through a Two Person Company and the Password 123456
item.description:
8,749,975 Danish ID numbers copied in about ten days. Names and home addresses, the dead included. One company with two employees. Its admin password: 123456. Found only when the invoice came.

The copied data holds names, home addresses and CPR numbers. The CPR number is the personal ID number Danes get at birth, or when they move to the country, and usually keep it for life. People who have died are in the data too, and so are people who moved abroad years ago. Denmark has about 6 million inhabitants. The register behind those numbers holds about 11 million records, and roughly 8.8 million of them were pulled out, according to the Danish digitalisation ministry.

The company the data went through is Pays ApS, a small software firm in Odense. In July 2026 it had two employees, according to the Danish business register. One of its services is what Danes call cpr-vask: cleaning up customer files against the national register, so that names and addresses are up to date.

For that work, the company had legal access to the register. Section 38 of the Danish CPR Act lets private companies look people up when they have a business reason, for example to find the current address of a customer or a member. The law asks the company to have identified each person individually beforehand, by CPR number or by name and address. Banks, telecom companies, insurers, law firms and trade unions have this kind of access. In total, 1,039 organisations do.

The story of how someone else got in comes from a person who says they did it. On Thursday evening, October 8, the Danish newspaper Politiken published its interview with the hacker. The paper spoke to them in English through an encrypted service, and received a file with 8,749,975 CPR records.

Its reporters put a description of the data and the method to several experts, and they all found it very likely that this person took part in the leak. One of them, Emil Hørning of the security company Defend Denmark, called the account credible and the method plausible.

The way in, according to the hacker, was the password of a former employee. That password had leaked earlier, and it was 123456.

The newspaper then did its own checking, and found at least three profiles at the company that used 123456. One of them was the administrator account, the account that can manage the others.

The company’s director and owner confirmed that its legal access to the CPR system had been abused. She declined an interview through her lawyer, and did not answer the newspaper’s questions about the company’s security.

Each lookup in the register costs money, and the CPR office bills the companies for them. On Friday evening, October 2, staff were preparing the invoice for this company. They saw an amount that a department head at the ministry later described at a press briefing as very, very large. Behind it were more than 14 million lookup attempts, made over about ten days in September. The company told the CPR office it had not made those lookups itself.

Documents seen by the Danish broadcaster TV 2 show that the access was in use from September 10. It stayed open for 21 days and 17 hours. The lookups appear to have stopped around September 20. By the time the invoice showed what had happened, whoever made them had been gone for twelve days. Jens Myrup Pedersen, a cybersecurity professor at Aarhus University, said the attacker got what they wanted and then left on their own. He also pointed out that there was no working system to spot the unusual activity.

The register itself is run by DXC Technology, a US company the Danish state hired to operate the CPR register and handle its IT security. The broadcaster has tried to get an answer from the company since October 6, and it has not replied.

14 million attempts against a register of about 11 million records. The ministry’s 8.8 million is the number of lookups that came back with a person. The broadcaster explained the gap: you can also search for numbers that do not exist.

That gap makes sense once you know how a CPR number is built. It has ten digits. The first six are the birth date: day, month, and the last two digits of the year. The seventh digit, read together with the year, tells which century the person was born in. The tenth digit is even for women and odd for men. Statistics Denmark describes the structure in its own documentation of the register.

A person born on 4 March 1985 has a number that starts with 040385. Four more digits follow. For one birth date, that leaves at most 10,000 possible numbers, and many of them were never given to a person. Numbers like that return nothing, which is how a search ends up with more attempts than there are records.

A program that wants most of the register can start from a date instead of a list of names. It tries the possible numbers for that date, keeps the ones that return a person, and moves on to the next day.

In its notice of October 5, the Danish Data Protection Agency writes that the register reported a very large number of automatic lookups, made to find out which CPR numbers are valid. The police have not described the method yet. One detail the hacker gave fits that description too.

AI wrote the program, the hacker told the newspaper. It is more than 40,000 characters long, and two experts who looked at the code for the paper concluded that it was indeed AI-generated. According to the hacker, any AI model launched in the past year could have done it. The hacker denied having strong technical skills.

As an example, the hacker pointed to a bug. The program searched for people born in 1877 instead of 1977, and because of that, people born in 1977 are missing from the file the hacker shared. In a CPR number, 1877 and 1977 have the same first six digits for the same birthday. Only the seventh digit sets the century apart. A program that got the century wrong for one year skipped the Danes born in 1977 who were in the register.

You can change a leaked password in a minute. A CPR number stays. The same documentation says a number is never handed out a second time. Getting a new one is rare. It happens, for example, when the birth date or sex was registered wrong, or after a legal change of gender.

The minister for digitalisation, Christina Egelund, called the breach deeply serious and said it was too early to say whether people will get new numbers. Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said it was an incident that should not have been possible.

Danes use the CPR number for public services, healthcare, tax and banking. Companies accepted it as a sign that the person on the other side was who they said they were. Laila Reenberg of Styrelsen for Samfundssikkerhed, the Danish agency for societal security, said you cannot use the number on its own to authorise anything, buy something or get sensitive personal information. She told companies and authorities to stop accepting a CPR number on its own as proof of who someone is.

What the copied data does give a criminal is a convincing start. A phone call or an email from someone who already knows your full name, your address and your ID number sounds like your bank or the tax office. The ministry warned about exactly that on the day it announced the breach. Never give out passwords or other confidential information by phone or email, it said, also when the person seems to know your name, address and CPR number.

Danes took that warning seriously. On October 5, the day the breach was announced, about 1,000 people called the national cyber hotline, against about 150 on a normal day. The government advice site sikkerdigital.dk had 180,000 visits against about 400. A credit warning is a flag that tells lenders to check extra carefully before they give credit in your name. The number of people who had one went from a little under 250,000 on October 1 to about 970,000 on October 7.

On Friday October 9, the CPR office sent a letter to the 1,039 organisations with access. It repeated the security rules they already had to follow. Each needs someone responsible for security and has to check regularly which employees still have access. It also has to keep an eye on how many lookups it makes each month.

Taking that access away is not simple either. The Confederation of Danish Industry, DI, warned that limiting what companies can look up in the register could make their work more expensive and lead to more mistakes. They would have to collect and check the data by hand.

People who have died are in the data too, and so are people who moved abroad years ago. Denmark has about 6 million inhabitants. The register behind those numbers holds about 11 million records, and roughly 8.8 million of them were pulled out, according to the Danish digitalisation ministry.

The company the data went through is Pays ApS, a small software firm in Odense. In July 2026 it had two employees, according to the Danish business register. One of its services is what Danes call cpr-vask: cleaning up customer files against the national register, so that names and addresses are up to date.

The law asks the company to have identified each person individually beforehand, by CPR number or by name and address. Banks, telecom companies, insurers, law firms and trade unions have this kind of access. In total, 1,039 organisations do.

The company’s director and owner confirmed that its legal access to the CPR system had been abused. She declined an interview through her lawyer, and did not answer the newspaper’s questions about the company’s security.

Each lookup in the register costs money, and the CPR office bills the companies for them. On Friday evening, October 2, staff were preparing the invoice for this company. They saw an amount that a department head at the ministry later described at a press briefing as very, very large. The register itself is run by DXC Technology, a US company the Danish state hired to operate the CPR register and handle its IT security. The broadcaster has tried to get an answer from the company since October 6, and it has not replied.

The seventh digit, read together with the year, tells which century the person was born in. The tenth digit is even for women and odd for men. A person born on 4 March 1985 has a number that starts with 040385. Four more digits follow. A program that wants most of the register can start from a date instead of a list of names. It tries the possible numbers for that date, keeps the ones that return a person, and moves on to the next day.

item.title: Ahold Delhaize Shut Down Albert Heijn and Five US Chains and Still Will Not Say What Happened
item.description:
77 million shoppers a week. On a Sunday afternoon, the company behind them switched off its own systems. Shelf labels showed last week’s prices. Six days later, it still has not said what happened.

I wrote about this in my newsletter on Friday. This morning, Saturday, the Albert Heijn website still shows an error page. I assume it was an attack. A company that big does not shut everything down for nothing. That is my opinion.

The company is Ahold Delhaize, based in Zaandam in the Netherlands. It owns Albert Heijn in the Netherlands, Delhaize in Belgium, and five chains in the United States. Its own website gives the size: 77 million customers a week, 9,551 stores and 384,000 employees.

On Sunday afternoon, October 11, Albert Heijn and its sister chains Etos and Gall & Gall switched off part of their own computer systems. The company said it did this to protect its IT systems. By Monday morning the website, the app and customer service were offline, and online orders could not be delivered. The personal discounts on the Bonus card stopped working, and so did the savings stamps and Air Miles. The stores stayed open and the tills kept working.

Albert Heijn stores use electronic shelf labels, small screens on the shelf that get their price from a central system. With that system off, the labels kept showing the offers of the week before. At the till, shoppers paid the current price, which was often higher. One store in Amsterdam put up a note to explain it. The labels showed the right prices again on Tuesday, October 13.

The stores get their goods from distribution centres, and those stopped too. At the distribution centre in Tilburg, the workers were sent home around noon on Tuesday. A driver told the regional broadcaster Omroep Brabant: “Nothing works. The systems are down.” Without those systems the staff could not pick the orders for the stores. All Albert Heijn stores in Belgium get their goods from that same centre, the Belgian broadcaster VRT reported, although the chain said the impact in Belgium stayed limited. In the Netherlands, shelves emptied, mostly dairy, vegetables and fruit.

In Belgium, Delhaize customers could not place new online orders, and customer service could not be reached. In the United States, the websites and apps of Food Lion, Stop & Shop, Hannaford, Giant Food and The Giant Company went offline on Monday, October 12. On Wednesday they were still down, and on Friday it was the fifth day in a row. American shoppers were sent to Instacart, DoorDash and Uber Eats instead. A spokesperson for that last chain told the Philadelphia Inquirer that if its app was still down on Friday, it planned to switch on all digital coupons on its customers’ loyalty cards automatically.

Employees felt it too. According to posts from staff on Reddit, quoted by BankInfoSecurity, Stop & Shop workers could not see their schedules or pay stubs in Kronos, their time-tracking system. Food Lion workers lost access to Spectrum, the company’s own platform for picking and handing out online orders. Food Lion staff were told to call it an “IT outage”.

On Monday morning, Ahold Delhaize put out a short press release. It was experiencing “a security issue within its network” and was “taking some systems offline to help protect them”. The same release carried a line meant for investors. It said the release contained news that can move the share price, what EU market rules call inside information. The public got “a security issue”.

On Tuesday, the company said it had “no evidence at this moment” that data of customers, employees or partners was taken, and that it had started to switch some systems back on in a controlled way. In an update on Wednesday, it added that it was working with its own teams, outside cybersecurity experts and the relevant authorities. It would not say more, because that could weaken its security or the way it responds.

In six days, the company has not called it an attack or a hack. Albert Heijn first spoke of an IT incident, and later of a cybersecurity incident.

On Tuesday, the public broadcaster NOS spoke to anonymous people in the security sector. According to them, the security staff at Albert Heijn saw suspicious attack traffic coming in, and switched the systems off while it was arriving. That, they said, stopped the attackers from getting deeper into the network. The traffic came through servers in the United States, Poland, Moldova and Turkey. Servers of Ahold’s own American branch may have been used as well, but that is not confirmed. Albert Heijn did confirm one thing: it shared details about the servers the attackers used with other companies.

Attackers rent servers in whatever country they like, or break into someone else’s server and send their traffic through it. A server in Poland shows the route the traffic took, and nothing about where the attackers are. The broadcaster made the same point. In cybersecurity, attribution, working out who is behind an attack, is one of the hardest problems.

Pim Takkenberg is a security specialist and a former police officer. On the current affairs programme Nieuwsuur he said: “It seems pretty clear to me that someone with bad intentions has been inside the system.” He thinks of criminals who are after money. He also told the broadcaster that the attackers may have broken into the American servers first, and attacked the Dutch systems from there.

On Friday, November 8, 2024, the American branch of Ahold Delhaize announced that it had detected a cybersecurity issue in its US network. It took some systems offline “to help protect them”. Hannaford stopped pickup and delivery orders for several days. The company said it had brought in outside cybersecurity experts and notified law enforcement.

Five months later, on April 16, 2025, the ransomware group INC Ransom put Ahold Delhaize on its leak site, a website where criminals publish what they stole from companies that do not pay. The group claimed up to 6 terabytes of stolen data. One day later, the company confirmed that files from its American systems had been stolen.

In June 2025, a notice filed with the US state of Maine put the number of people at more than 2.2 million. They were current and former staff and their family members. Depending on the person, the files held names, contact details and dates of birth, Social Security, passport and driver’s license numbers, bank account numbers and health information. In July 2025, one of them filed a class action against the company, a lawsuit on behalf of a large group of affected people, in a federal court in North Carolina.

The stolen files were not only about Americans. In April 2025, Ahold Delhaize said it suspected that data of staff in the Netherlands had been taken as well. It concerned people on the payroll in April 2021 at Albert Heijn, Etos, Gall & Gall and other parts of the group. According to the newspaper AD, that meant names, bank account numbers and the amount of their salary payment of early April 2021. Ahold reported it to the Dutch Data Protection Authority. This week, the anonymous sources pointed to servers of that same American branch.

Same company, same words, almost two years apart. Last time, the full picture came out five months later, after the criminals had put it on their own leak site.

A company can have reasons to say little while an investigation runs. A public statement can come back later in a lawsuit, or in the claim with an insurer, and since 2025 Ahold knows the first one from experience. Whether that is the reason now, the company has not said.

The Dutch police and the Public Prosecution Service did something unusual on Wednesday, October 14. They publicly invited Ahold to file a police report. Police rarely do that in public, the broadcaster noted.

Ahold did report the incident to the National Cyber Security Centre, as a new Dutch cyber law that took effect in August requires. That notice is not the same as a report to the police.

The police and prosecutors can also start an investigation on their own, without a report. They have not. Stan Duijf, who leads the police approach to cybercrime, explained why on the talk show Pauw & De Wit on Thursday. Albert Heijn says no sensitive customer data was lost, and he called that an important reason not to start one yet. He also said: “We say: do it as early as possible, because then we can actively start the investigation.”

The police call the first hours after an attack the golden hour. The longer it takes before investigators can start, the more traces disappear. With an investigation, the police can seize servers or search them to see what runs on an IP address.

In 2024, the American branch notified law enforcement from the start. This time, in the Netherlands, the police are relying on the company’s own word.

By Thursday evening, the company had still not filed a police report. On Friday, justice minister David van Weel said he understood that a company first focuses on protecting its systems, but that the time had come to file a report. He was also in contact with Frans Muller, the CEO of Ahold Delhaize, and pressed him for openness. A spokesperson said they could not respond to the minister’s words, Reuters reported.

Three estimates of the damage are going around, and they are far apart.

Cor Molenaar, emeritus professor of e-marketing at Erasmus University Rotterdam, put the damage for Albert Heijn at about 10 million euros, and warned it could grow fast the longer it lasts. He also thinks it was a DDoS attack, where many computers flood a system with traffic until it stops working. The other experts I found think someone got inside.

Retail expert Erik Hemmes calculated that Albert Heijn had missed about 21 million euros in revenue in its stores and online by Wednesday.

The financial paper Het Financieele Dagblad heard from people in the supermarket sector, who did not want to be named, that the crisis costs Ahold Delhaize tens of millions of euros a day. Ahold told that paper it was too early to say what the financial impact would be.

For scale: in the last three months of 2025, Ahold Delhaize sold for 23.5 billion euros. That is more than 250 million euros a day, for all of Ahold Delhaize together. Most of it comes through the tills in the stores, and those stayed open. Shoppers who could not order from Albert Heijn went elsewhere. Jumbo, Lidl, Picnic, ALDI and PLUS all told the news agency ANP that their stores were busier and they got more online orders.

On the stock market, the share fell almost 3 percent on Monday, the biggest loser in the Amsterdam AEX index that day, and then recovered. It closed at 32.36 euros on Friday. On November 4, Ahold Delhaize publishes its results for the third quarter, its first scheduled results since the incident started.

That same Sunday night, a few hours after the systems at Albert Heijn went off, attackers heated the fridges and freezers in hundreds of French supermarkets to 50°C. I wrote about that on Tuesday. Two incidents at supermarket groups in one weekend, and yet Ahold Delhaize and the NCSC both said they see no sign that the two are connected.

An intrusion into a company network usually starts at one weak point: a stolen password, or a server facing the internet that missed an update. The password often comes from a phishing email that tricks an employee into typing it on a fake page. From that first machine, the attacker looks around, to see which other machines are on the network and where the passwords are kept. The attacker collects those passwords and moves from machine to machine, until reaching the systems that run the business or hold the data.

In a ransomware attack, the data gets copied out first. Then the attacker encrypts the files on the machines, so the company cannot open them. The company now has two reasons to pay: to get its systems back, and to keep its data off a leak site.

This is why security staff pull systems off the network the moment they see attack traffic. An attacker sitting on one machine needs the network to reach the next one. Cut the connections, and the attacker is stuck. The company is stuck too. At Albert Heijn the tills kept working, but the distribution centres, the app and the deliveries did not. Days of empty shelves and more than a week of cancelled orders are the price of not letting someone go further. The company says it has no evidence so far that anything was taken.

As of Friday evening, Albert Heijn had cancelled all online orders up to and including Tuesday, October 20, and new orders still could not be placed. Customers who already paid will be compensated once the systems work again. Deliveries should start again in the second half of next week. Customer service is still unreachable. The shelves are full again.

On November 4 the company talks to its investors. Until then, a leak site may say more than Ahold Delhaize does.

That, they said, stopped the attackers from getting deeper into the network. The traffic came through servers in the United States, Poland, Moldova and Turkey. Servers of Ahold’s own American branch may have been used as well, but that is not confirmed. Albert Heijn did confirm one thing: it shared details about the servers the attackers used with other companies.

Attackers rent servers in whatever country they like, or break into someone else’s server and send their traffic through it. A server in Poland shows the route the traffic took, and nothing about where the attackers are. The broadcaster made the same point. In cybersecurity, attribution, working out who is behind an attack, is one of the hardest problems.

Pim Takkenberg is a security specialist and a former police officer. On the current affairs programme Nieuwsuur he said: “It seems pretty clear to me that someone with bad intentions has been inside the system.” He thinks of criminals who are after money. He also told the broadcaster that the attackers may have broken into the American servers first, and attacked the Dutch systems from there.

On Friday, November 8, 2024, the American branch of Ahold Delhaize announced that it had detected a cybersecurity issue in its US network. It took some systems offline “to help protect them”. Hannaford stopped pickup and delivery orders for several days. The company said it had brought in outside cybersecurity experts and notified law enforcement.

Five months later, on April 16, 2025, the ransomware group INC Ransom put Ahold Delhaize on its leak site, a website where criminals publish what they stole from companies that do not pay. The group claimed up to 6 terabytes of stolen data. One day later, the company confirmed that files from its American systems had been stolen.

In June 2025, a notice filed with the US state of Maine put the number of people at more than 2.2 million. They were current and former staff and their family members. Depending on the person, the files held names, contact details and dates of birth, Social Security, passport and driver’s license numbers, bank account numbers and health information. The stolen files were not only about Americans. In April 2025, Ahold Delhaize said it suspected that data of staff in the Netherlands had been taken as well. According to the newspaper AD, that meant names, bank account numbers and the amount of their salary payment of early April 2021. Ahold reported it to the Dutch Data Protection Authority. This week, the anonymous sources pointed to servers of that same American branch.

Same company, same words, almost two years apart. Last time, the full picture came out five months later, after the criminals had put it on their own leak site.

A company can have reasons to say little while an investigation runs. A public statement can come back later in a lawsuit, or in the claim with an insurer, and since 2025 Ahold knows the first one from experience. Whether that is the reason now, the company has not said.

The Dutch police and the Public Prosecution Service did something unusual on Wednesday, October 14. They publicly invited Ahold to file a police report. Police rarely do that in public, the broadcaster noted.

The police call the first hours after an attack the golden hour. The longer it takes before investigators can start, the more traces disappear. With an investigation, the police can seize servers or search them to see what runs on an IP address.

In 2024, the American branch notified law enforcement from the start. This time, in the Netherlands, the police are relying on the company’s own word.

By Thursday evening, the company had still not filed a police report. He was also in contact with Frans Muller, the CEO of Ahold Delhaize, and pressed him for openness. A spokesperson said they could not respond to the minister’s words, Reuters reported.

Three estimates of the damage are going around, and they are far apart.

Cor Molenaar, emeritus professor of e-marketing at Erasmus University Rotterdam, put the damage for Albert Heijn at about 10 million euros, and warned it could grow fast the longer it lasts. He also thinks it was a DDoS attack, where many computers flood a system with traffic until it stops working. The other experts I found think someone got inside.

Retail expert Erik Hemmes calculated that Albert Heijn had missed about 21 million euros in revenue in its stores and online by Wednesday.

The financial paper Het Financieele Dagblad heard from people in the supermarket sector, who did not want to be named, that the crisis costs Ahold Delhaize tens of millions of euros a day. Ahold told that paper it was too early to say what the financial impact would be.

For scale: in the last three months of 2025, Ahold Delhaize sold for 23.5 billion euros. That is more than 250 million euros a day, for all of Ahold Delhaize together. Most of it comes through the tills in the stores, and those stayed open. Shoppers who could not order from Albert Heijn went elsewhere. Jumbo, Lidl, Picnic, ALDI and PLUS all told the news agency ANP that their stores were busier and they got more online orders.

On the stock market, the share fell almost 3 percent on Monday, the biggest loser in the Amsterdam AEX index that day, and then recovered. It closed at 32.36 euros on Friday. On November 4, Ahold Delhaize publishes its results for the third quarter, its first scheduled results since the incident started.

That same Sunday night, a few hours after the systems at Albert Heijn went off, attackers heated the fridges and freezers in hundreds of French supermarkets to 50°C. I wrote about that on Tuesday. Two incidents at supermarket groups in one weekend, and yet Ahold Delhaize and the NCSC both said they see no sign that the two are connected.

An intrusion into a company network usually starts at one weak point: a stolen password, or a server facing the internet that missed an update. The password often comes from a phishing email that tricks an employee into typing it on a fake page. From that first machine, the attacker looks around, to see which other machines are on the network and where the passwords are kept. The attacker collects those passwords and moves from machine to machine, until reaching the systems that run the business or hold the data.

In a ransomware attack, the data gets copied out first. Then the attacker encrypts the files on the machines, so the company cannot open them. The company now has two reasons to pay: to get its systems back, and to keep its data off a leak site.

item.title: LG Smart TVs Could Be Taken Over From the Same WiFi Without a PIN
item.description:
Three bugs chained in order gave an attacker full control of a smart TV, straight over the home WiFi, without the set ever asking for its PIN. The owner did nothing wrong. A demo app that ships on the TV, and a test certificate it still trusted, were enough to reach root.

Root is the account that sits above everything else on the machine. With it you can read what is on the TV, change any setting, install software, and switch the hardware on and off.

The person who got there did not touch the remote and did not know the owner’s account. What they needed was a place on the same network. A guest who got the WiFi password once, a phone in the house with a bad app on it, or a laptop that was already infected. Any of those is close enough.

A smart TV sits in the corner and plays Netflix. Underneath it is a computer with its own operating system, and it can be attacked like any other.

LG calls that system webOS. By the company’s own count it runs on more than 200 million LG televisions. This attack was built and shown on two of them.

An independent researcher showed it at TyphoonPWN 2026, a live hacking contest in Seoul run by a company called SSD Secure Disclosure. At a contest like this, a researcher brings a working attack, runs it on stage against the device, and gets paid if it lands. The prize pool reaches into the hundreds of thousands of dollars.

This one took third place in the LG category. The researcher chose to stay anonymous, and the full writeup went public on October 12.

It was tested on two sets, the LG 32LQ636BPSA and the 27TQ600SW. Both ran webOS 7.5.7-25 on firmware 04.54.40. They are small sets, a 32-inch and a 27-inch, the kind that end up in a kitchen or a bedroom. How far it reaches past those two, the research does not say.

Start with how the TV is supposed to stay safe.

To run the TV from your phone, you use LG’s ThinQ app, and the two have to be introduced first. The TV shows a code on the screen. You type that code into the phone. Only then does the TV trust it.

That on-screen code does one job: it proves the phone is in the same room as the person with the remote, and not someone sitting out on the network.

webOS also keeps its apps apart, so a small app cannot reach in and call the services that run the television. Three mistakes take all of that apart, one after the other.

The first mistake is about that code.

These TVs ship with a small built-in app called sync-demo. It is the kind of app that runs on a demo set in a shop. Inside it sits a pairing file, signed by LG itself so the TV knows it is genuine.

The attacker copies that signed file and sends it to the part of the TV that handles pairing. Two things go wrong at the same time.

The file asks for a permission called STB_INTERNAL_CONNECTION. The TV reads that as a connection it already trusts from the inside, so it decides no code needs to be shown.

Someone signed that file with a test certificate, the kind developers use on the workbench. A TV in a living room should never have trusted it. This one did.

So the TV skips the code and hands back a key at its highest level of trust.

One key is not full control yet. The second mistake widens the opening.

Another built-in app, cmp-client, can be told to open a web page. It takes the address of that page from whoever starts it.

Before it opens the page, it runs one weak check. It asks the address whether it is there, and if it answers, the app loads it. It never checks where the address actually points.

So the attacker points it at a page of their own.

What makes this serious is where that page runs. It runs inside a trusted app, and it keeps that app’s line to the services deep inside the TV. A web page the attacker wrote can now call controls that an outside connection is never allowed to touch.

The third mistake runs the command.

The TV has a service that collects log files, called pmlogd. One of its jobs asks for the name of a folder to put the logs in, and it builds a system command out of whatever name it is handed. It drops that name into the command without cleaning it first.

Send it an ordinary folder name and nothing happens. Send it a folder name with an extra command added on, and the TV runs the extra command too.

pmlogd runs as root. So the command runs as root.

Put the three together and the path is short: skip the code, reach the service that was supposed to be out of reach, and run a command as the most powerful user on the machine. The researcher’s proof ends with the TV printing uid=0. That is the system’s own way of saying you are root.

A rooted TV is a foothold inside the house.

From there an attacker can look across the home network and find the router, the laptops, the phones and the other smart gadgets, and go after those too. They can leave their own software on the set, quiet and out of sight, and use the TV as one more machine in a botnet that attacks other people. They can reach the accounts you signed into on the set.

Earlier work on webOS by security researchers listed the same risks: move sideways through the network, pull the TV into a botnet, or watch the owner.

Most of the news stopped at one line: three bugs, no CVE. LG’s own security bulletin tells more.

In its September update, labelled SMR-SEP-2026, LG lists five problems, not three. LG rates all five High. All five landed on the same day, June 18, 2026, and LG credits them to SSD Secure Disclosure.

Three of them are the ones in the public writeup: the hard-coded secret in sync-demo, the weak address check in cmp-client, and the command injection in pmlogd.

The other two never made the writeup. One is a way past the login check in the second-screen gateway service. The other lets an attacker gain higher rights through the first-time setup screen.

So “no CVE” is true in one narrow way. These did not get numbers from MITRE, the body that hands out CVE numbers. In any practical way it is wrong. LG runs its own list, which it calls LVE, and on that list the flaws were logged, numbered and fixed.

One detail is easy to miss.

That second-screen gateway service, the one with the login bypass on this year’s list, is the same service Bitdefender broke in 2024. Back then, one of their bugs, CVE-2023-6317, slipped past the security PIN in that service and created a privileged account with no action from the owner. A second, CVE-2023-6318, ran commands as root.

Two years later, a different team, the same two moves: get past the check that proves you belong, then run a command as root. The service even carries the same name.

That 2024 round was not small either. The firm found four flaws across webOS versions 4 through 7. When they searched Shodan, the search engine for devices connected to the internet, they counted more than 91,000 TVs with the weak service open to the public internet. It was only ever meant for the home network.

LG fixed those in 2024. And it keeps happening at this one contest. A year earlier, at TyphoonPWN 2025, another researcher took first place in the LG category with a different chain. That one walked out of a folder it was locked into and read the stored keys of phones that had paired with the TV.

The living-room set has become a regular target in Seoul.

The limits matter too. Only those two sets were tested, so how far the chain reaches across other webOS 7.5 models is not something the research settles.

The attacker has to be on the same network as the TV. Someone has to be past the router already, on a network the TV trusts by default. The open internet does not reach it directly.

And LG has pushed a fix, on its TV security bulletin page. A set that is up to date, and off the affected firmware, is not open to this chain.

LG says it sends security updates to a webOS platform for five years after that platform first ships. A set older than that window eventually drops off the list, which is worth checking if the TV in the room has a few years on it.

What you can do:

  • → Update your TV’s firmware now, and turn on automatic updates so the next fix arrives on its own
  • → Look at what is connected to your home WiFi, and drop anything you do not recognise
  • → Put your smart TV and other smart-home gear on a separate guest network, away from your phone and your computer
  • → Treat the local network as something that can be reached; a guest’s phone sits on it too
  • → If a TV does not need the internet for what you watch on it, there is no harm in taking it off the network
  • → In the TV’s settings, turn off the microphone and voice features if you do not use them

item.title: Discover-Tech Ads Delivered Zero-Click Spyware to Al Jazeera While Google Approved the Company for Six Years
item.description:
Spyware got onto Al Jazeera devices through an ad that only had to load on the screen. 45 were targeted, and the owners did nothing wrong. The company behind the ad ran code on 120,768 websites, approved by Google for six years.

On October 15, two teams published the same finding on the same day. Researchers at the Citizen Lab in Toronto and the ad-security company Confiant laid out the first clear proof of something security people had warned about for years: spyware that lands on a phone or a laptop through an ordinary online ad. There was no link to click and no file to download. They gave it a name, AdFection.

The usual warning is about shady links you should not click. This one had nothing to click. The ad only had to appear on the screen. The moment it loaded, a small piece of code inside it reached out to a server and asked one question: is this the person we are looking for? If the answer was yes, the attack ran. If the answer was no, the server sent back nothing, and the reader scrolled on, never knowing an ad had checked who they were.

The company at the center of this is Discover-Tech, an Israeli firm registered in 2020. On paper it looked like any other advertising business. The books say otherwise. In four months it spent only about 109,000 dollars, the records show almost no income from selling ads, and more than a third of its budget went to promoting its own website.

It bought ad space in the same automated auctions that fund most of the free internet. And it was trusted. From 2020 until this month, Discover-Tech sat on the lists of certified and approved ad vendors kept by Google and by IAB Europe, the trade body for the industry. For six years this was a vendor in good standing. Google cut its access in early October and said it did so “for systematically violating our policies.” The trade body dropped it around the same time.

To see how an ad can carry an attack, it helps to know what happens in the half second before any ad appears. When a page or an app opens a slot for an ad, it does not pick one in advance. It holds an auction. Dozens of companies get told what device you are on and where you are, tagged with a code called your advertising ID that follows you from app to app. They bid, live, for the right to show you something. The highest bid wins, and its ad drops into the slot. This happens hundreds of billions of times a day, and it is over before the page has even settled.

Discover-Tech bid in these auctions like any other buyer. But some of the ads it won carried something extra. The instant the ad rendered, a line of code phoned home to a Discover-Tech server and handed over your advertising ID and IP address, along with the cookies on the page. The server checked those details against a target list. If your device was not on it, the reply was exactly zero bytes. If it was, you got a block of code that ran on the spot. Because the server stayed silent for the rest, the scanners that are supposed to catch bad ads had nothing to flag.

The targeting was a product, not a one-off. On Discover-Tech’s platform a customer could pick a single person by advertising ID, by browser, or by IP address, and push a chosen ad straight to that one device. Clients could run it under their own branding and limit a campaign to a single country.

The scale is the part that is hard to sit with. Between March and June of this year, the researchers counted Discover-Tech bidding on 3.77 billion ad slots and winning about 442 million. Ads carrying its code showed up in 75,373 apps and on 120,768 websites, across 161 countries. At least 718 million of those bids carried the hidden code that calls home.

The heaviest targeting landed on conflict zones and small states. Yemen drew 457 million bids. In Montenegro the ads were aimed at people more than 150 times over, counted per head of population. Confiant’s cofounder Jerome Dangu put it at 10 million ads a day, and said very likely hundreds of millions of people were touched by Discover-Tech. In the Palestinian territories, he said, the ads were hard to avoid. Most of those ads were ordinary. But the same channel that carried a harmless Sudoku ad to one phone carried spyware to a target on another, and from the outside the two looked the same.

It was not only far away. In the Netherlands, 1 in 54 ads shown on iPhones came from Discover-Tech. Belgium was the single most-targeted country Confiant counted, 56 percent of all the hits, first seen on April 12.

A second trick makes it worse. Ad companies swap data with each other through something called cookie matching, a quiet arrangement that lets them recognize the same person across different sites. item.title: Siemens Software Center Ran Attackers' Code With a Valid Siemens Signature on PCs That Never Installed It
item.description:
Canon, then Stardock, now Siemens. Attackers keep running their code behind a trusted signature. On October 19 Siemens confirmed its own signed program was the latest, on Windows PCs that never had it.

Here is what it looked like on a PC that got hit. A program called Siemens Software Center, sitting in the list of apps that start with Windows. On a machine that never had Siemens software on it. The owner did not put it there. It loaded on its own at startup.

That program is genuine. Siemens makes it, and its customers use it to download, install and update the software they bought from Siemens. It even carries Siemens’ own digital signature, which tells Windows “we made this file, and it has not been changed.” Both of those things were true here. The file was genuine. The signature checked out. And it was running the attacker’s code.

Siemens confirmed all of this on October 19.

So how does a genuine, signed program end up on a machine that never asked for it, running someone else’s code? It takes two steps, and I will walk through both.

The first step is how it landed on the computer at all. The trick is called ClickFix, and I wrote about it on October 3. It goes like this. You open a web page, and the page tells you something needs to be verified or fixed. It asks you to press Win+R, paste in a line it gives you, and hit Enter. What you cannot see is that the page already dropped a command onto your clipboard. Win+R opens the little Run box in Windows, the one that runs whatever you put in it.

You think you are proving you are human. In that one paste, you run the attacker’s command, on your own PC, with your own account.

That is why the Siemens warning carries one line meant for ordinary people and not for IT staff: never paste a command from a web page into Win+R, the Run box or PowerShell.

That pasted command pulled in an installer called AllMyBasic.msi from a server the attackers controlled. The installer made a folder named SM Software Provisioning Service in a corner of the user’s own account, and dropped the original SiemensSoftwareCenter.exe inside it. Right next to that file it placed its own, among them one called archive.dll. Then it gave the program a spot in the startup apps, so it comes back after a reboot.

And that one extra file, lying beside the original one, is the attack itself. To see why, you need one small thing about how Windows programs are put together.

A program is almost never a single file. Around the main program sit smaller helper files, called DLLs, that hold pieces of the code the program leans on while it runs. When the program needs one, it asks Windows for it by name. Windows then looks in a fixed order, and the first folder it checks is the one the program was started from. The first file it finds with the right name wins. It does not ask who made it.

So the attackers gave their file the name the program was looking for and left it in that same folder. The program asked for its helper, grabbed the attacker’s file instead, and ran it. There was no warning. The security world calls this DLL sideloading. Siemens logged it as CVE-2026-110936, in the family of bugs known as an uncontrolled search path.

The signature on SiemensSoftwareCenter.exe vouches for that one file, and nothing else. It says Siemens made it and it was not tampered with, and that stayed true throughout. It says nothing about archive.dll sitting beside it. So the moment the program loaded that DLL, the attacker’s code was running inside a process Windows saw as trusted Siemens software. That is exactly why they picked this program. Siemens said so plainly: they chose it because it is signed and trusted.

On paper the bug does not even look frightening. Siemens scores it 8.4 out of 10 on the newer scale and 6.7 on the older one, and the fine print assumes the attacker is already on your machine with high rights, ready to drop that DLL. But in these attacks the person dropping the DLL is you, by pasting the one command that brought it in.

Siemens is not the first brand used this way, and the warning was already out there.

On September 28, researchers at Huntress laid out a run of attacks that, for some victims, began with a Google search for the word chatgpt. A paid result at the top pointed to a custom assistant hosted on the genuine chatgpt.com. Talk to it, and it gave the same answer each time: the service is busy, please use our backup page. The backup page was a fake Cloudflare check, and the check asked you to paste a command. The same ClickFix move.

That command installed a fake printer tool built around a genuine program signed by Canon, and used it to sideload the attacker’s DLL, the same trick used on Siemens. A later wave swapped Canon for a program signed by Stardock. Both ended in the same place: a remote access tool that hands over the screen, the camera and the microphone, and comes with a file manager that searches through the contents of the files on the PC. Huntress counted at least 40 incidents.

And they do not sit still. The first fake assistant came down on September 25. Two days later there was a new one. By October 14 they had fresh web addresses in rotation, like gptverification[.]com. Take one down, another is already up.

In that same report, back in September, the researchers wrote plainly that it was highly likely other signed programs were being abused the same way, and that any alarm built on those two names would miss the next one. Three weeks later, the next one carried a Siemens signature. And the Siemens flaw was reported to the company by Jose Oregon of Huntress Labs, from the same team behind that report.

The second connection comes from Forescout. On October 15, the same day the Siemens advisory came out, its researchers published a write-up of something called ROMULUS. They had been working a separate case and noticed the malware was coming from a server running a login panel by that name. ROMULUS turned out to be a ready-made delivery system for ClickFix attacks: one web address hands a victim a PowerShell script, another hands over an installer, and on one of the servers a stats page quietly counted installs and runs by country.

They found it on six servers. One of them, 2.27.248[.]127, is the exact server Siemens named as the one that handed out the AllMyBasic.msi bundle with the signed program inside. Another, 96.62.224[.]81, is the one behind the fake chatgpt assistant. The same servers, three different signed brands.

Who runs ROMULUS is still an open question. Forescout is careful about it: it could be one private crew, a service other criminals rent, an affiliate setup, or a tool that got copied around. What we can be sure of is how the malware works and which server sent it, not who is behind it.

This is also not the first time Siemens Software Center had a DLL problem. Back in August 2023, Siemens disclosed the same class of flaw in the same program, CVE-2021-41544, reported by a researcher at Dragos and fixed in version 3.0. Three years on, the same weakness turned up again in a newer version, 3.5.8.7, and this time someone put it to use.

On October 17 Siemens added the fix, version 4.0.9.8, to its advisory. If you already run Siemens Software Center for work, you do not have to do anything, because it updates itself the next time you open it. That closes the hole for the people who actually use the program.

It does nothing about the copy the attackers carry. Their bundle brings its own old 3.5.8.7, with the genuine signature still on it, drops it in its own folder, and never goes near Siemens’ official download. Siemens has said nothing about pulling back the certificate behind that signature. Its own advice points the same way: do not rely on the file’s fingerprint, because the file is Siemens’ own and the fingerprint matches. Watch the folders and the behaviour instead.

Siemens lists these signs of trouble, for users and for defenders:

  • → Siemens Software Center in your startup apps or Task Scheduler on a PC that never had it installed
  • → A folder called SM Software Provisioning Service in AppData\Local\Programs
  • → SiemensSoftwareCenter.exe running from AppData\Local\Programs, started by msiexec
  • → The files activate.bak or statinfosta.DB next to SiemensSoftwareCenter.exe
  • → A folder called FTSuite with a file called ftc.uml in AppData\Local
  • → Connections to 96.62.218[.]59

You can check the two folders yourself in PowerShell, run as the user who might have pasted the command:

1
2
3
4

Test-Path "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Programs\SM Software Provisioning Service"
Test-Path "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\FTSuite\ftc.uml"
Get-ScheduledTask | Where-Object { $_.TaskName -like "*Siemens*" }
Get-CimInstance Win32_StartupCommand | Where-Object { $_.Command -like "*Siemens*" }

The two Test-Path lines answer True or False. A True on either one, or a Siemens entry in the last two lines on a PC with no Siemens software, means the machine needs a closer look.

For the people who run the network, Siemens gives the indicators to block and to search the logs for:

1
2
3
4

Active:   96.62.218[.]59 and wizardexpensive[.]com (payload hosting and C2)
Inactive: 2.27.248[.]127 (distributed AllMyBasic.msi)
AllMyBasic.msi  SHA-256 f4d7c5321bb0d1bda439304a753bcf9b467b98ca53c7e9493b9c2c3451092e4a
archive.dll     SHA-256 3fdcc7d7d049a89711fb31fb236940a1c5a09d899143ffd20c3c41fb1f2cf491

The inactive server is down now, but a machine that pulled from it earlier can still be infected. Siemens also says to look for unexpected DLLs next to Siemens programs outside the normal install folder.

If a PC matches, Siemens says to take it off the network, stop the process, remove the startup entry and the scheduled task, and reset the passwords, before the usual incident response. Change the passwords used on that machine first, from a different device.

Siemens says it knows of no break-in to its own systems, products or update channels, and that the attackers spread the signed program together with their own files outside the official channels. The company is sharing what it knows with the authorities and with security vendors. The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security put out its own warning, AV26-1063, the same day. There are no victim numbers, and no name has been put to the attackers.

A signature covers one file, the one it is attached to. It says nothing about the other files that program pulls in while it runs.

Want to see what is starting up on your own Windows machine, and spot the one entry that does not belong? That begins with understanding how programs load and where things hide. 2
3

item.title: PHP2Shell Flaw Leaves Millions of Websites Open to Takeover
item.description:
More than 22 million PHP installations sat exposed online this week, facing two flaws that need no password. The details leaked before a patch existed. Updating WordPress does not fix it. The flaw is in PHP itself, the back end of most of the web.

On Tuesday, October 20, details of two unpatched holes in PHP started spreading online. A post on Hacker News announced that someone would disclose the bugs on October 22, with no patch ready. The post came down, but the screenshots had already gone around, including one of an exploit tool called PHP2Shell. Security firm watchTowr looked at what leaked and confirmed the flaws were genuine and allowed remote code execution. PHP had planned a quiet, scheduled fix. Instead it had to put one out while the details were already public.

The PHP team set an emergency release and said it might ship sooner if attacks appeared. Cloudflare reported early attacks against PHP sites on Wednesday morning and rolled out firewall rules to blunt them. The patch arrived in the afternoon, a little earlier than the planned 14:00 UTC release.

You could see how seriously people took it by what went dark. In the Netherlands, the site digid.nl, the government’s main login, showed a plain page: this website is temporarily unavailable. MijnOverheid went down with it, and so did the website of the national parliament and the site of the cyber agency, the NCSC, the people whose job is to warn the public. Logging in with DigiD on other services still worked, but its own site, and plenty of others, were gone. Tweakers and Security.NL, two of the country’s best-known tech sites, were offline as well.

It reached far past one country. Reuters reported that government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline on Wednesday, with agencies in Finland among those that pulled their sites as a precaution. Cybersecurity agencies in Europe, Australia, Japan and Britain told PHP users to update at once or take their sites offline until they could. The EU’s CERT-EU said much the same: patch the moment a fix exists, and where that is not possible, consider cutting internet-facing applications off from the public internet until it is.

In Germany, Freiburg University took its central websites offline at 10:39 that morning, along with its intranet, the ILIAS learning platform and webmail for student addresses, and told its departments to pull their own PHP systems too. None of these were confirmed break-ins. They were organisations deciding it was safer to be unreachable than to keep running a version of PHP that someone could take over.

To understand why a government would rather go dark, you have to know where PHP sits. PHP runs the back end of most of the web. W3Techs puts it at 69.3% of all the sites whose server-side language it can identify, and WordPress, which by itself runs nearly 40% of all websites, runs on it. So do Magento for shops, Drupal and Joomla for larger sites, phpBB for forums, WHMCS for hosting billing, and MediaWiki, the software behind Wikipedia. None of those applications contains the bug. It sits in the PHP underneath them, so you can write a site perfectly and it is still exposed.

The release fixed two separate problems. The first, CVE-2026-109618, lives in the way PHP handles running out of memory. When a request uses too much memory, PHP jumps out of whatever it was doing to shut that request down cleanly. The trouble is that the memory for a request is sometimes reachable before it has been fully set up. If an allocation fails at that moment, PHP does not account for the early exit. The cleanup step then works on data that was never valid, and a carefully built request can turn that confusion into running the attacker’s own code on the server.

What makes it practical is how easy that out-of-memory moment is to force. PHP reads the body of a form upload, the multipart/form-data type a browser sends when you attach a file, before your application code ever runs. A request that never declares a usable length can slip past the post_max_size limit meant to stop oversized uploads. Empty file fields do not count against the max_file_uploads cap, yet PHP still builds the full set of internal records for each one. Combine enough of those and memory runs out on command, at the exact spot where the first bug lives.

The second flaw, CVE-2026-109619, is a different kind of mistake. A PHP worker keeps some state in memory between requests, things like error and session data. PHP should wipe that state before it hands the memory back. A fatal error, including one from that same out-of-memory trick, can skip the cleanup. PHP frees the memory while the worker still points at it. The next request reads a pointer to memory that no longer belongs to it. That is a use-after-free, and with the right heap layout it too ends in code running with the web server’s own privileges.

This weak spot is not new. In 2004, the researcher Stefan Esser found the first remote bug in the way PHP handles its memory limit. In 2020, a bug report flagged the same out-of-memory behaviour around file uploads. In 2024, a security audit by OSTIF and Quarkslab found a related memory problem, though researchers could not prove it was exploitable at the time. The two flaws patched today are where that long-running weakness finally turned into a working attack.

PHP rated both flaws 9.2 out of 10, critical but not a perfect score. The number reflects that the attack is not trivial: it takes high complexity and the right conditions to line up. Some early reports threw around a 10.0; the official rating is 9.2. It is still an unauthenticated attacker, reaching in across the internet, ending with code running on the server. The gap between 9.2 and 10.0 means little when proof-of-concept code is already public.

One detail in the advisory matters if you run a server. For the first bug, PHP’s own analysis proved the full attack over HTTP on Apache with mod_php, the classic setup where PHP runs inside the web server, on default settings. It calls PHP-FPM, the setup many managed hosts use, susceptible too, though no complete exploit of that first bug has been shown against it. The second bug changes the picture. PHP says the session route reached working code execution on both mod_php and FPM, so FPM is not the safer option it might look like. Both setups need the patch now.

The flaws did not come from attackers. They were reported to the PHP team, which worked on a fix before the details were meant to be public. The repair is in the core of PHP. The developers took out the risky jump-out-on-low-memory step at the root of the first bug, and made the worker clear its leftover state properly to close the second. That is what today’s release fixes.

The patched versions are:

  • → PHP 8.5.12
  • → PHP 8.4.27
  • → PHP 8.3.36
  • → PHP 8.2.35

Anything below those is vulnerable. PHP 8.1 and older no longer get updates from the PHP project, and one scan on October 20 found around 884,000 internet-facing servers still running 8.1 or older. The PHP team put out minimal backports for 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1 for people who build PHP from source, but anything past that is on its own. In India, one scan counted 19,847 servers on versions that no longer get security fixes. And PHP 8.2, the oldest branch still supported, reaches end of life on December 31, 2026, so sites on it should patch now and plan the move to a newer version.

Different scanners give different totals, but they point the same way. VirusTotal fingerprinted around 5.1 million internet-facing addresses running PHP. Palo Alto’s own scan flagged more than 22.6 million instances as potentially vulnerable. The exact figure matters less than what it shows: PHP is one of the most widely installed pieces of software on the internet, on millions of servers at once. Security officials put what exposure means in plain terms. A server that gets taken over can have its data stolen, its logins broken and its pages pulled down.

If you run a WordPress site, this is the part that catches people out. Updating it does not close the hole, and neither do your plugins, because the fix is to PHP, which lives on the server underneath them. The same goes for any PHP application, whatever it runs on. The only thing that matters is the version of PHP your host runs, and whether they have updated it. If you do not manage your own server, the only fix is the one your host installs, so ask your hosting provider to apply the PHP update now.

The good news is that checking where you stand takes a minute. On your own server you can ask PHP its version:

1

php -v

One catch: that shows the command-line PHP, which is not always the version your website runs. Check what the site itself reports, for example with php-fpm8.3 -v or a phpinfo page. If it comes back below 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27 or 8.5.12, you are exposed and need the patch. After updating, restart PHP-FPM or Apache, because workers that are already running keep the old code until you do. On shared hosting where you cannot run any of this, the safer move is to contact your host today and ask one question: have you applied the October 21 PHP security release. The configuration tweaks going around, like turning off session upload progress, only block one path and do not make the server safe. Only the patch closes the hole.

A newer version number is not always proof you are safe. Distributions often patch by backporting the fix into a package that still shows an older version, so the number alone can mislead. The surer check is the package changelog. On Debian or Ubuntu, running apt changelog php8.3-cli lists the recent changes; on Red Hat systems, rpm -q --changelog php does the same. If one of the two CVE numbers shows up there, the fix is in. If it does not, the package has not been touched yet, whatever the version says.

Whether attackers are already using this against live sites is not clear. Cloudflare saw attack attempts against PHP sites on Wednesday morning, and hosting companies reported the same. As of October 21 there was no confirmed break-in: the Dutch cyber agency said it had seen no active abuse, and neither flaw appeared yet on the US government’s list of known exploited vulnerabilities. Unit 42 said it had seen proof-of-concept code, not a live intrusion. By late afternoon the patch was out, a little before the planned 14:00 UTC release, though many sites that had gone dark stayed down into the evening.

What took government websites offline in country after country was a flaw that had sat in the most common software on the web for years, until the day its details leaked. Public proof-of-concept code is out now, and after a leak like this, mass scanning usually starts within hours. If you own anything that runs PHP, a blog, a shop, a forum, a company site, what counts now is whether your server was patched before someone came looking.

Do you know which version of PHP your own site runs on, and what an attacker sees when they scan it from the outside?
