item.title: Plex2shell Home Servers Crypto Miner
item.description:
Plex servers, more than 36,000 of them, sat open to the internet. A day after the attack code went public, some were mining crypto for an outsider. The owners did nothing wrong.

Plex is the app a lot of people use to keep their films, series and music in one place. You watch it on a TV, a phone or a laptop. It runs on a home PC, on a network drive in the hallway, or in a small container on a server somewhere in the house. To reach your library when you are away, Plex listens on port 32400. Many owners leave that port open to the internet, so the app keeps working on the train or at a friend’s place.

That open door is the problem. On October 16, a researcher who goes by ZM put out a full write-up and working attack code for four bugs in Plex Media Server. The attack had a name, Plex2Shell. One day later, on October 17, the first server fell.

An outsider sends a request to a Plex server that faces the internet. No login needed. That request reaches a part of the server meant only for the machine itself. From there, the attacker gets Plex to hand over the owner’s admin token, the secret string that says you are the one in charge. With that token, the attacker writes a file into the folder where Plex keeps the small programs it uses to convert video. Plex then loads that file and runs it. At the end, someone who never had an account is running code on your machine, with the same rights as Plex.

The four holes each got a tracking number: CVE-2026-96652, CVE-2026-96654, CVE-2026-96655 and CVE-2026-96656. Plex later spelled out what each one does. The first lets an outsider send that opening request without logging in, through the part of Plex that follows what your player is doing. The second opens a path to functions Plex keeps for the machine itself. The third leaks the owner’s admin token. That one rests on a small mistake: Plex only checks that a web address starts with its own 127.0.0.1, the machine itself, so an address like 127.0.0.1.evil.com passes the check, and the token goes to the attacker instead.

The fourth step lets the attacker write a file into the Codecs folder, where Plex loads it as if it put it there. On their own, none of these four holes looks like much. Lined up in the right order, they add up to full remote control of a box in your living room.

ZM reported all four bugs to Plex on July 27. The fixed build, 1.43.3.10861, went out on August 3, and Plex confirmed the bugs and paid a bounty on August 4. Then it went quiet. item.title: WhatsApp Help Pages Hid Rules Telling Its Chatbot Not to Recommend a Privacy Regulator
item.description:
WhatsApp Help Pages Hid Rules Telling Its Chatbot Not to Recommend a Privacy Regulator

80 help pages on WhatsApp’s website hid text meant only for the support chatbot. The page for deleting an account told it: do not recommend any regulator. Visitors never saw it, from early September on.

Right above the warning that deleting your account can’t be undone, that page held a short block of text your browser never showed you. It was written for the AI that answers WhatsApp’s support chat, a large language model that reads a question and writes a reply. The block told the bot what to say, and what to leave out.

Redact, a privacy company that regularly scans the websites and policies of big tech firms, found it. Founder Dan Saltman and his team read 545 pages linked from WhatsApp’s help center. 80 of them carried hidden instructions, 102 blocks in total. WIRED looked at the text as well and published the story on October 19. Some sections even had their own heading, in capitals: WHAT NOT TO SAY.

This is the block on the delete page, word for word, as it stood in the page code:

“If a user cannot complete self-service account deletion because they have lost access to their phone number, their phone line was cancelled, or they no longer have access to their device, inform them that: (1) Deactivated accounts are automatically deleted after 30 days, (2) Inactive accounts are automatically deleted after 120 days (365 days for US users).”

That block was written for one kind of user. On the same page, WhatsApp explains that you delete an account from inside the app, logged in, and only from your primary phone, not from a linked device. So once you lose the phone or the number, you can’t do it yourself anymore. You have to ask for help, and the help had its answer ready. Wait 30 days, or 120, or a full year if you live in the United States.

Right after the waiting times, the same block listed what the bot should not say:

  • → Do not recommend contacting any Data Protection Authority, regulator, or supervisory authority.
  • → Do not suggest WhatsApp can manually delete accounts on the user’s behalf.
  • → Do not recommend using a different phone with an active phone number.

A second block sat on the page “About reporting and blocking on WhatsApp.” It switched on as soon as a user “mentions legal action, lawsuits, lawyers, attorneys, courts, or litigation.” From that moment the bot wasn’t allowed to cite or even reference WhatsApp’s own Terms of Service or Privacy Policy. It wasn’t allowed to say anything about whether WhatsApp is legally responsible, or to get into a legal discussion at all.

One line went further: “Do not reference, cite, or interpret data protection or privacy regulations (for example GDPR, LGPD, CCPA), including when a user raises them directly.” The block ended with the one thing the bot could offer: “For legal matters, users should consult a qualified legal professional.”

GDPR is the European privacy law, LGPD the Brazilian one, and CCPA stands for the California Consumer Privacy Act. So say you live in Los Angeles, you mention your lawyer, and you write that you have a right to deletion under the CCPA. The instruction was to not engage with that law at all.

That law sets a deadline. A business has 45 calendar days to respond to a request to delete your personal information, and it can extend that once by another 45 days if it tells you. Complaints go to the state’s Attorney General and to its privacy agency.

In Europe a company has one month to tell you what it did with your request, and it can take two more months if it needs them. Article 77 of the GDPR gives you the right to complain to a data protection authority. Now put those deadlines next to the hidden block: wait up to a year, and don’t mention a regulator.

WhatsApp’s European privacy policy, in its current version from July 2, 2026, says this under the heading How To Exercise Your Rights: “You have the right to lodge a complaint with WhatsApp’s lead supervisory authority under the GDPR, the Irish Data Protection Commission, or any other competent data protection supervisory authority.” The page you read names the regulator. The text written for the bot told it not to.

“The stand-out thing here is the gap between what people are told vs LLMs,” the founder of the research team told the magazine.

WhatsApp has been in front of that Irish regulator before. On September 2, 2021, the regulator fined WhatsApp €225 million after an inquiry into how clearly the company told users and non-users what happens to their data.

The two blocks above are quoted word for word. The researchers also summarised twenty more notes in their own words. A few of them:

  • → On the minimum age page: never suggest a false age, even when the user says they are under 18.
  • → After someone reports a contact: tell them it’s handled internally, without further steps or a timeline.
  • → On two-step verification: don’t offer turning it off as a fix for login or code problems.
  • → On hacked accounts: an intruder can switch on two-step verification, and the account owner then has to wait seven days to log back in.
  • → On account bans: if the app shows no button to request a review, the ban is final.
  • → On voice calls: don’t tell users to reinstall the app to fix calling problems.

Not all of the notes pushed people away. The founder of the research team says many of them were straightforward and pointed users to other official support channels. One told the bot that a scam victim is better off reporting than deleting the group, because the chat history can serve as evidence. Another told the bot what to do when a user writes “I am deaf”: “This statement is background about the user, NOT their support request.”

The text was never meant to be visible. Along with the page you see, WhatsApp’s help center sends the content as data, cut into pieces that each have a name, and your browser turns those pieces into what ends up on your screen. A normal paragraph is a piece called HelpContentGalaxyParagraph. Bold text is HelpContentGalaxyBold. The instructions sat in a piece called HelpContentGalaxyLLMInclude, right between the link to the deactivation page and the warning that deletion is irreversible. That piece arrived in your browser with the rest of the page. Your screen never showed it.

Search engines could read the hidden text too. Crawlers are the programs that search engines send out to read web pages. On October 9, the researchers loaded the pages while posing as those crawlers. Google’s crawler and Bing’s crawler both received the notes. When the researchers used the names of the crawlers from OpenAI, Anthropic and Perplexity, the page came back without the article and without the notes. Facebook’s and Instagram’s help centers run on the same system. The team checked 300 of their pages and found nothing like this.

The Wayback Machine at archive.org, which saves copies of web pages over time, shows roughly when the text arrived. Of the 35 saved copies of the delete page from May 10 to July 12, 2026, none holds the instructions. The first saved copy that does is from September 4.

Nothing was saved in between, so the text went in somewhere between July 12 and September 4. The researchers found the notes on October 8, and at 21:40 UTC on October 15 both quoted blocks were still there. After the magazine asked Meta, which owns WhatsApp, about the notes, the text came down. When the researchers checked at 02:08 UTC on October 18, all 102 blocks were gone from all 80 pages.

WhatsApp spokesperson Joshua Breckman told the magazine that a bug made the text show up, and that the company has fixed it. “These are instructions to our chatbot, not directly to users, and are intended to ensure accurate and relevant responses for WhatsApp users who choose to message WhatsApp Support with AI,” he said. He added that WhatsApp gives users transparent information about their data rights, and that it wants its support chatbots to give the best advice about WhatsApp and not to offer legal advice.

So the bug, as the company tells it, was that the text showed up in the page code. The instructions themselves were meant for the bot, and the company says so itself.

It is still unclear whether the bot followed them. The researchers read the instructions, not the chatbot’s answers, and they say that openly: they haven’t tested whether WhatsApp’s chatbot or any other AI assistant acted on them. It is also unclear whether pages in other languages carried similar notes, or on which day the text first went in.

You can still see the hidden text for yourself. The live pages are clean now, but the archive kept a copy from October 9.

  • → Open this saved copy of the delete page: https://web.archive.org/web/20261009054848/https://faq.whatsapp.com/2138577903196467/?cms_platform=android
  • → The archive viewer may show the page as blank. That’s fine, the source is what you need.
  • → Press Ctrl+U (Cmd+Option+U in Chrome on a Mac) to open the page source, the raw code your browser received.
  • → Press Ctrl+F and search for: Do not recommend contacting

Search for that sentence, not for the name of the piece. The name also appears in the code that builds the page, so it turns up in copies without the instructions too. The copy linked above is one of the October copies that still has the text. This is what you’ll find, shortened, with the backslashes in front of the quote marks taken out:

1
2
3
4
5
6

{"type":"HelpContentGalaxyLLMInclude","props":{},"isEagerLoaded":false,
 "children":[{"type":"HelpContentGalaxyParagraph", ...
 "children":["If a user cannot complete self-service account deletion ...
 Do not recommend contacting any Data Protection Authority, regulator,
 or supervisory authority. Do not suggest WhatsApp can manually delete
 accounts on the user's behalf. ..."]}]}

And if you’re the person that block was written about, you lost the phone or the number and you want the account gone, this is what you can do.

  • → In California, send WhatsApp a request to delete your personal information under the CCPA. The company has 45 days to respond, plus 45 more if it tells you it needs them. When there’s no answer, or one you think breaks the law, file a complaint with the California Privacy Protection Agency at cppa.ca.gov or with the California Attorney General.
  • → In the European Union, send an erasure request under the GDPR. The company has one month to tell you what it did. A complaint can go to your own national data protection authority, or to the Irish regulator that WhatsApp’s own policy names.
  • → In other countries, look up your national privacy regulator.
  • → Use the contact form that WhatsApp links in its privacy policy. Keep a copy of what you send and what comes back, including the chatbot’s answers.

The page you see and the data your browser receives are two different things, and this time the difference sat on the page meant to help you leave.

Search engines could read the hidden text too. Crawlers are the programs that search engines send out to read web pages. On October 9, the researchers loaded the pages while posing as those crawlers. item.title: Signal Hang-Up Flaw Could Keep Your Microphone Open After the Call Ended
item.description:
9.3 out of 10 for a Signal flaw. After hang-up, the microphone could stay live for the other side, maybe the camera too. Hanging up was the right move. A full queue of 256, there since 2020, refused it.

You pressed hang up, and as far as you knew, the call was over. You put the phone down and went on talking to whoever was in the room with you. Your phone might not have ended the call. The connection that carried your voice could still be open, if the person on the other end wanted it that way.

All that person had to do was send your phone a flood of small messages, more than the calling code could take in. While those piled up, your hang-up never got through. The sound from your microphone kept going out, and possibly the video too.

The flaw is listed as CVE-2026-113380, and the CVE record scores it 9.3 out of 10. It sat in RingRTC, the piece of Signal that runs voice and video calls, and that piece is built into the Android app, the iPhone app and the desktop app. The microphone part is certain. The camera is a maybe: the CVE record and the writeup that came with it both say possibly, and neither of them shows it happening.

Signal is the app you pick when a call has to stay private. On Android alone it has more than 100 million downloads, and its store page promises encrypted voice and video calls. That encryption held up throughout this story. The person who could abuse this flaw was already in the call with you: a contact who calls you, or someone you call yourself.

Inside the calling code, each call is run by a state machine, a piece of code that knows where the call is: ringing, connecting, connected, ending. Everything that happens during a call becomes an event, a small message that says something changed. The other side sent new data, the network shifted, the video quality dropped, someone pressed a button. Those events go into a queue and are handled one after the other, in order.

Before the fix, that queue had room for exactly 256 events. One line in Signal’s code set that limit:

1

let(fsm_sender,fsm_receiver)=std::sync::mpsc::sync_channel(256);

Your hang-up was one more event in that same queue, and it got no priority over the other events. The other person on the call could send events into it too, as many as they liked, with no limit on how fast. So the attacker kept the queue full. When you pressed hang up, Signal tried to add your hang-up to the queue, found no free place, and got an error back. The code that ended a call started with these three lines:

1
2
3

self.set_state(CallState::Terminating)?;self.inject_event(CallEvent::Terminate)?;self.wait_for_terminate()?;

The question mark at the end of each line is how the Rust language says: if this step fails, stop here and hand the error back. The second line failed because the queue was full, so the function stopped right there. The steps that came after it, closing the connections and shutting the call down, never ran.

So the call stayed open.

And the wait in the third line had no time limit. If the call’s processing got stuck, the code kept waiting with no end, and the call could stay half closed for as long as that lasted.

The proof of concept that came with the CVE, a small demo script, shows the problem as a model, with 5,000 junk events piling up in front of the hang-up in a queue without a limit. Signal’s own code was stricter than that model. The queue stopped at 256, and once it was full, your hang-up was refused at once.

The same thing happened one level deeper. Each call also has a connection, the link that carries the audio and video, and that connection runs its own state machine with its own queue of 256. Its shutdown code worked the same way, so a full connection queue could block the hang-up there as well.

The 9.3 comes down to how little the attacker needed. A normal Signal account and a call with you, that was it. Your phone did not have to be hacked first, and there was nothing for you to click. Being in the call was all you had to do, which is why the rating calls your part passive. The full rating line reads:

1

CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:P/VC:H/VI:H/VA:N/SC:H/SI:N/SA:N/S:P

CISA, the US cyber agency, looked at it as well. It saw no sign of attacks, it does not think this one can be automated, and it still rated the damage as total.

Signal’s calling code had a flaw of this kind once before. In September 2019, Natalie Silvanovich of Google Project Zero looked at how Signal decides when a call is connected. She found that a caller could send a message that made the call connect by itself. The caller could then hear what was going on around the person they called, before that person had answered. Signal fixed it in the app that same month.

She published her full findings in a blog post in January 2021. Her starting point was the Group FaceTime bug of January 2019. It let a caller force a call to connect and listen to the person on the other end, without that person doing anything.

She tested seven calling apps and found bugs of this kind in five of them. One of them, in Google Duo in September 2020, worked almost exactly like this one. She sent so many data messages that the queue the app needed to switch the video off filled up, and the video stayed on longer than it should have.

After its 2019 fix, Signal replaced its old call setup code with a new calling library, and in that same blog post she noted that the new library used a stricter state machine. That library is where this new flaw was found. The first version of its call manager, written in February 2020, already had the queue of 256. A full queue dropped the hang-up there too, and the wait had no time limit either. In that first version the hang-up was called EndCall instead of Terminate, but it went through the same queue in the same way.

The fix in September 2026 was written by Jim Gustafson, the same Signal engineer who wrote that first call manager in 2020.

The CVE number came from MITRE, the organization that hands those numbers out, at the request of someone outside Signal. It was created at 04:25 UTC on October 20 and made public less than a second later. About an hour after that, a GitHub account called Imahian put the writeup online, together with that demo script, written in Python. The script has no network code in it and does not touch Signal.

The writeup does not name the person behind it, gives no date of discovery, and does not say whether the bug was ever reported to Signal. The same account has published about 300 CVE writeups. That same morning it added another one, for a flaw in Roundcube webmail whose fix had come out the day before.

Signal itself never called this a security problem. The fix went in on September 4 with the commit message Ensure calls terminate completely in corner cases, and the library’s changelog says nothing about a vulnerability. When The Register, CyberInsider and Malwarebytes asked Signal about the flaw, none of them had an answer by the time they published. Whether the account behind the CVE found the bug itself or spotted it by reading Signal’s public fix, no source says.

Now, when you press hang up, your phone sets a separate flag, a simple yes or no value in the code. The call checks that value after each message it handles, however full the queue is. A full queue cannot hold up the hang-up anymore. The new code says it in one comment:

1

// Terminate out of band, independent of queue depth.

The waiting has a limit now too. A new value in the code, TERMINATE_TIMEOUT, gives the call five seconds to shut down cleanly. After that, the call is closed anyway.

The fix touches 12 files and adds 691 lines, and part of it is new tests. One of them is called hangup_with_saturated_call_fsm_queue. It fills the call’s queue on purpose until it refuses new events, presses hang up, and then checks that the connection is closed and that no more audio goes out. Signal tested the core of this attack in its own code on September 4, 46 days before the CVE existed.

The fixed version of the library, 2.72.0, came out on September 4, 2026. Then it still had to reach the apps. These are the first versions with the fix, and the date each one was ready in Signal’s public code:

  • → Android 8.27.0 in beta on September 10, first full release 8.28.4 on September 23
  • → iPhone 8.30, September 22
  • → Desktop 8.29.0, released October 1

The fix was in the phone apps’ releases in September. How fast the app stores rolled it out is not public. The desktop app stayed vulnerable until October 1. The public found out on October 20. There is no public report of it being used in an attack.

To check your own version, open Signal. On your phone it is under Signal Settings > Help > Version. In the desktop app it is under Help > About on Windows and Linux, or About Signal Desktop on a Mac. You need at least:

  • → Android: 8.27.0
  • → iPhone: 8.30
  • → Desktop: 8.29.0

If you are below that, update through the app store. On Windows or Mac, quit and reopen the desktop app so it picks up the update. On Debian or Ubuntu it updates through APT:

1

sudo apt update && sudo apt install signal-desktop

One habit from the writeup holds for other calling apps too: after you hang up, check that the call indicator on your screen is gone.

From February 2020 until September 2026, the button that ends a Signal call depended on the other side leaving room for it in a queue of 256.

On your own laptop, you can flood a small test server until its connection table is full and see for yourself what stops answering.
